results.title: Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Remodel Capitalism
results.author: Antara Haldar
results.content:
Democrats Have a Historic Opportunity to Rethink Capitalism
The model actually exists. Politics just needs to catch up.
“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.
The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?
“The barbarians are inside the gate,” Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson wrote on X in July in the wake of a slew of primary victories by progressive candidates. By splitting the Democratic Party and inviting the ire of Republicans, these insurgents became a defining force in the U.S. midterms, with candidates such as James Talarico and Annie Andrews winning unlikely Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina, and Peggy Flanagan and Manny Rutinel clinching victories in Minnesota and Colorado, respectively. The formal adoption of a resolution condemning socialism recently in the House of Representatives and U.S. President Donald Trump’s warnings about the “communist menace” as fundamentally un-American on the country’s 250th anniversary signal how seriously the challenge was taken this past summer, even as—amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis and growing disillusionment with the economic system—the concept of democratic socialism has become more palatable to American voters.
The verdict at the polls this week is a referendum on not just a highly consequential political contest, but also a historic battle of ideas. Having breached the gates, can this new wave of progressives change the architecture of U.S. capitalism?
On the left, politicians associated with democratic socialism, most prominently New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, have revived ideas once consigned to the margins—stronger labor institutions, higher minimum wages, universal healthcare, higher taxes, and a wider social safety net including paid family leave and government-funded preschool and college. At least 11 midterm races were decided on these issues, including the closely watched Senate race in Michigan won by Abdul El-Sayed.
But on the right, Trump, too, by introducing tariffs and returning to industrial policy, has thrown the conventional economic playbook out the window and eschewed the free-trade impulses that traditionally characterized Republican economics.
The two movements are perceived to be almost completely at odds. But what unites them is that they are—fundamentally—reactions to the economic consensus that has been dominant since the Cold War. Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who along with former U.S. President Ronald Reagan ushered in capitalism’s era of dominance, described its global embrace with the pithy phrase: “There is no alternative.”
The political scientist Francis Fukuyama subsequently coined a grand formulation to describe the alliance between free market economics and liberal democracy as an elixir of economic and political life: the “end of history.” The economic proposition that underlay it, known as neoclassical economics, proposed to replace the faltering human touch with the “invisible hand.” Built around the belief that markets could coordinate millions of strangers, it promised to convert private interest into public benefit. Without requiring shared values or common purpose, it not only relied on the rationality of the price mechanism to allocate every resource to its best use but also promised to diminish inequality.
The system succeeded in delivering global growth on an unprecedented scale, roughly tripling the world economy in size, yet the model’s blind spots have become increasingly harder to ignore. The imperfections of the price mechanism that treats carbon as a negative externality and children a positive one, but fails to put a value on either, are becoming more glaring. Collective-action problems, such as the alignment problem presented by artificial intelligence and climate change, demonstrate that individually rational choices can produce collective outcomes that are highly irrational. And inequality has increased, particularly within countries, even as aggregate output has grown.
Most fundamentally, around the world, the human psyche is instinctively rejecting the desiccated account of human nature as solitary and narrowly self-interested, on which economics is premised, and the institutions built around these assumptions that leave people feeling increasingly alienated.
Unsurprisingly, Gallup finds that confidence in U.S. institutions is near an all-time low. In that sense, both the populist right and the progressive left are rebellions against the attempt to shoehorn humans into the role of the relentlessly utility-maximizing Homo Economicus, or Economic Man, at the heart of the narrative of economics.
Flesh-and-blood people may respond to incentives, but they equally value emotion and social connection. Yet capitalism’s scaling logic has relentlessly favored speed and size. The result has been banks that are too big to fail, “Big Tech” that concentrates power and sets off antitrust alarms, and global supply chains whose efficiency can tip rapidly into fragility. The drive for economic growth quickly outpaces the human capacity for trust.
By contrast with the proportions of most of our economic institutions, the famous Dunbar number shows that each human being can sustain roughly 150 stable relationships. At the same time, a growing body of research establishes that cooperation and reciprocity are economically salient patterns of behavior defining our relationships.
Our institutions are simultaneously too small to contend with problems on a global or planetary scale—think of climate change, artificial general intelligence, financial contagion, global poverty, and pandemics—and so are, ethically and functionally, suboptimal on a cognitive level. Yet our nation-states, domestic economies, and corporations are too large to feel affectively meaningful.
So, what if, instead of building ever-larger institutions ever faster, we built “affective institutions” that acknowledge the human capacity for fellow feeling, engage the “moral machinery” or finer feelings, and aggregate them into consensus-based communities?
Elinor Ostrom’s Nobel Prize-winning scholarship illustrates, through examples such as forests, fisheries, and irrigation systems around the world, that community governance structures can rival markets and governments by deploying locally constructed norms to create robust economic communities.
Her findings are often considered quaint because of the constraint on institutional size that they impose, but new breakthroughs in network science provide a possible answer to the problem of scale. Dense communities where reputation and repeated interaction matter can be linked through threads or bridges that connect those communities, allowing information, capital, and successful practices to travel between them. The resulting architecture is a latticework of fishnets connected through fireworks, a system that is cohesive but not centralized, balancing local trust and large-scale reach.
Real-world models of what these “affective institutions” might look like already exist. Mondragon’s cooperatives in the Basque region of Spain combine locally governed, largely autonomous enterprises embedded in a shared financial structure. The group employed more than 71,000 people and recorded more than $12 billion in sales in 2025, serving as a significant proof of concept.
The 27-country-strong European Union, whose membership includes previously warring nations, represents a much larger, more ambitious experiment. Indeed, its structure, based on the principle of subsidiarity—which holds that decisions should remain at national, regional, or local level unless they can be achieved more effectively at the EU level because of their scale or effects—suggests a more useful economic approach than whether government should be bigger or smaller: At what level should each problem be solved, and how should those levels connect?
This new blueprint is of direct relevance to progressives across the United States. After America’s socialist summer, the question is whether the collective effervescence of the movement can congeal into something that can be sustained.
If the “warmth of collectivism” spreading from New York’s experiment with Zohranomics is to spark a revolution that tackles not just the crisis of affordability but also human agency, then the right scaling technology, built around citizens, consensus, and resilience, will be key. The midterms present a historic opportunity to turn widespread voter disaffection away from the self-destructive nihilism of the Make America Great Again movement and toward constructive agency. That will require moving beyond the stale market-versus-state binary and building structures rooted in individuals, embedded in communities, and linked through diffuse but connected networks. The scientific breakthrough has already happened; the politics just needs to catch up.
Few projects could be more faithful to the American promise than putting people—and the relationships between them—back at the center of economic and social life. Progressives now have a chance to stop being cast as the “barbarians at the gate” and storm the political citadel instead. But to do that, they will need to remodel the architecture of U.S. capitalism, by human hand.
results.summary:
A new wave of progressive politicians is challenging the traditional U.S. economic consensus, seeking to reshape American capitalism by prioritizing community-based institutions over conventional market-driven growth models.

### Key Points
- Progressive candidates, including James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Peggy Flanagan, and Manny Rutinel, secured notable victories in recent midterm elections.
- Democratic socialist figures like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders are advocating for universal healthcare, higher minimum wages, and expanded social safety nets.
- The movement draws inspiration from Elinor Ostrom’s research on community governance and the Mondragon cooperative model in Spain.
- Critics, including Republican Speaker Mike Johnson and Donald Trump, have labeled these progressive economic proposals as socialist threats to American values.
- The proposed "affective institutions" aim to balance local trust and human connection with the large-scale reach required to address global issues like climate change.

### Why it Matters
This shift represents a fundamental challenge to the neoclassical economic consensus that has dominated U.S. policy since the Cold War. By moving beyond the traditional market-versus-state binary, these political movements aim to address widespread voter disillusionment and the growing alienation caused by current economic structures.

results.title: Singapore Airlines is Latest Global Carrier to Be Caught Up in Massive Amadeus Data Breach
results.author: Paddle Your Own Kanoo
results.content:
WHAT TO KNOW
- Around 46,000 bookings have been affected by the data breach.
- The breach could have been ongoing for more than three years.
- More than a hundred global airlines use the Amadeus system to manage flight bookings.
Singapore Airlines has revealed that it has been caught up in a massive data breach at a third-party vendor, with around 46,000 bookings affected by the leak. Passenger names, booking reference numbers, travel itineraries, and booking classes have been illegally accessed, although credit card information and other personal information were not compromised.
Six global airlines have now admitted to being victims of the data breach. Along with Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific has confirmed that 53,000 passenger records were illegally accessed; Japan Airlines, with 92,000 records leaked; and ANA All Nippon Airways said 37,800 passenger records were accessed.
In addition, Korean Air and Germany’s Condor have also admitted to being victims of the data breach, although neither revealed the extent of the information accessed.
The third-party vendor is Amadeus, which supplies around 130 airlines worldwide with its full-service passenger technology platform, Altéa.
Altéa runs flight booking and management systems, as well as check-in, revenue management, and even flight management and operations. Essentially, many of the services that passengers use on an airline’s website are being run in the background by Amadeus.
The data breach is understood to have taken place over a more than three-year period between August 2023 and September 2026, when Amadeus finally became aware that its system had been compromised.
Amadeus has taken action to ‘mitigate’ the breach and carried out a password reset to lock out nefarious actors.
Airlines have been on high alert for potential cyber breaches since early 2025, when security experts warned that hackers like the infamous Scattered Spider (also known as Muddled Libra) were attempting to gain illegal access to secure airline databases.
Hackers don’t necessarily use lines of code to break into secure systems as you might see in the movies, and are instead employing ‘social engineering’ scams to trick IT support desks into giving them legitimate login credentials to a company’s computer systems.
With access to booking data and a passenger’s email address, hackers could use the information to attempt a phishing scam.
This is where scammers send their victims an email that looks like it came from the airline or another legitimate company. Phishing scams normally try to get victims to click on a link within the email that will usually do one of two things:
- Clicking the link will install malware on the victim’s computer, which can then be used by hackers to view sensitive information like bank login data.
- Or it will redirect victims to a fake website designed to look like the airline’s own site, whereby passengers hand over personal details which can then be used by the fraudsters.
Has Singapore Airlines had a data breach?
Yes. Around 46,000 Singapore Airlines bookings were affected by a data breach at a third-party vendor, Amadeus.
What passenger data was accessed?
Passenger names, booking reference numbers, travel itineraries and booking classes. Credit card details were not compromised.
Which airlines are affected by the Amadeus data breach?
Six airlines so far:
Singapore Airlines (46,000 bookings)
Cathay Pacific (53,000 records)
Japan Airlines (92,000 records)
ANA All Nippon Airways (37,800 records)
Korean Air
Condor
What is Amadeus Altéa?
Altéa is Amadeus’s passenger technology platform, used by around 130 airlines. It runs booking, check-in, revenue management, and flight operations systems behind many airline websites.
How long did the data breach last?
It is understood to have run for more than three years, from August 2023 until September 2026, when Amadeus discovered it.
What should affected passengers watch out for?
Phishing emails that look like they come from the airline. Clicking a link in one of these emails may install malware or lead to a fake airline website built to collect personal details.
Related
Mateusz Maszczynski honed his skills as an international flight attendant at the most prominent airline in the Middle East and has been flying ever since... most recently for a well known European airline. Matt is passionate about the aviation industry and has become an expert in passenger experience and human-centric stories. Always keeping an ear close to the ground, Matt's industry insights, analysis and news coverage is frequently relied upon by some of the biggest names in journalism.
results.summary:
A massive data breach at travel technology provider Amadeus has exposed the booking information of passengers across six major global airlines, including Singapore Airlines and Japan Airlines.

### Key Points
- The breach affected approximately 46,000 Singapore Airlines bookings, alongside records from Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, ANA All Nippon Airways, Korean Air, and Condor.
- Compromised data includes passenger names, booking reference numbers, travel itineraries, and booking classes, though credit card information remains secure.
- The unauthorized access occurred within the Amadeus Altéa platform, which supports booking and operations for roughly 130 airlines worldwide.
- Security experts identified that the breach persisted for over three years, spanning from August 2023 until its discovery in September 2026.
- Hackers reportedly gained access through social engineering tactics, tricking IT support staff into providing legitimate login credentials.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks posed by third-party vendors that manage critical infrastructure for the global aviation industry. Passengers should remain vigilant against sophisticated phishing attempts that leverage stolen booking details to distribute malware or harvest additional personal information.

results.title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
results.author: Cosmos Institute, Jessica Hullman
results.content:
This is a guest essay by Jessica Hullman, Ginni Rometty Professor of Computer Science and Policy Fellow at Northwestern University.
In his essay on the role that rigorous proofs play in mathematical advances, Bill Thurston writes that the measure of success in math research is “whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics.” Many recent discussions of AI for science hinge on a tension between understanding and answers. Is science about humans achieving insight, or the archiving of verifiable solutions?
One side prioritizes outputs. Progress is implied to be evident in verifiable proofs of longstanding conjectures and cures for diseases, whether humans were involved in their making or not. The other side argues that human understanding is paramount, because it drives integration of new findings into the canon, because it shapes and inspires the next generation, and so on. But the first side, those who emphasize correct outputs, dismisses this as gatekeeping or nostalgia.
When Terry Tao posed a thought experiment in a recent talk, asking how comfortable people would be taking a cancer treatment produced by AI, complete with a formal certificate of correctness and a passed phase 3 trial, but without any human understanding how it was found, critics suggested that Tao’s reasoning missed the point. Of course a patient with stage 4 cancer would welcome the treatment.
Other examples concern ambiguity in authorship. Tom Dietterich wrote about arXiv’s growing problem with papers submitted by human authors who seem unlikely to have the expertise to understand the claims. Many questioned in response why accountability – by which I mean being answerable for a claim, able to describe what it rests on and respond when it’s challenged – should matter if verification has been solved. I suggested peer reviewers reserve their expert judgment for texts that don’t get flagged as heavily AI-written, so as to prioritize review as human exchange, but some see this as an obstruction to truth-seeking rather than an attempt to preserve it.
The problem is that if we all agree that outputs matter–that we do care about the solutions to longstanding conjectures, that we do ultimately want to know how to cure diseases–then understanding appears as something separate. It’s cast as a mental state that looks optional next to the cure or the proof itself, and becomes easy to dismiss as a second-order constraint that we tack on because historically we’ve required it to arrive at the solutions in the first place.
When defenders of understanding don’t dispute this separation, they immediately lose the argument. It becomes easy for the side that prioritizes output to peg them as simply not trying hard enough to envision a new future. But the superficial framing of understanding that we keep falling back on obscures deeper concerns that these examples share. They are less about anyone’s mental state than about what happens when something goes wrong. Tao’s scenario turns on the possibility that the AI passed the trial by exploiting a weakness in the trial itself. A paper whose authors can’t explain its claims leaves no one to consult if those claims fail.
Where along the way did we come to believe that scientific value lies in correctness alone?
This intuition is ultimately less about AI than it appears. The inclination to let AI drive science is less a sign of how forward-thinking one is about our future with AI, and more a symptom of a “value-free ideal” that has shaped our thinking since the Cold War era: a view that only epistemic criteria (not ethical and social values) deserve a place in judging what the evidence shows. That it pervades our debates about AI for science is not so surprising; it’s only in the last few decades or so that rejecting the value-free ideal became the philosophical mainstream.
This ideal feeds unrealistic expectations and keeps us from seeing that pushback against the rapid infiltration of AI output into the scientific record is neither anti-AI nor anti-science. The stakes are bigger than any one debate or field. The value-free ideal distorts how we go about seeking truth, causing us to mistake verified results for knowledge. It threatens the human capacities that sustain science, causing us to see criticism and accountability as inconvenient overhead rather than the mechanics of knowledge production. It leaves us confused about what understanding is, and consequently why it matters.
Is science “naturally aligned”?
The social contract for science represents an idealized relationship between science and society that arose after World War II in the US: scientists receive public funding and autonomy, and in return society receives the benefits of their inquiry. Built on a distinction between pure and applied science and a “linear model” in which basic research feeds applied work, the social contract replaces abstract arguments about the value of understanding with practical societal benefits, reshaping how we see science. Drawing on arguments made by concerned scientists in the late 1800s, who worried public celebration of new inventions like electric lights and the steam engine would crowd out respect for what they viewed as their more essential contributions, it also helped to forge a value-free ideal that says that at its core, science must be removed from “contextual values” like ethical or social concerns. For the social contract to gain broad societal buy-in as a model of scientific progress (and consequently shore up government investment in scientific research), we needed to imagine truth-seeking as the impersonal application of methods, immune to political or social pressures.
Philosophers of science aspired to inquiry based only on “epistemic” (or “cognitive”) values. Any influence from the scientist’s intentions or values came to be seen as a risk that the right methods should minimize, laying the groundwork for today’s questions about why it should matter who asserted the claim so long as it’s correct.
Many debates about AI’s role in science come down to disagreements about whether the scientific truth can be realized purely through use of the right procedures. Over the course of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there was almost a moralizing drive to eliminate as much of the scientist’s self as possible from the scientific process, so that trust in individuals could be replaced with trust in the system.
AI agents set loose on the scientific literature, able to verify and intervene experimentally themselves, look like the long-awaited fulfillment of nineteenth century scientific ethics. Much of the “AI for science” rhetoric inherits what I call the “science is naturally aligned” premise: by enacting the scientific method at scale, with its various justification procedures, we can reach a place where we no longer need human judgment to produce truth.
Is what is true really so separable from understanding or accountability? Math has become a centerpiece in recent debates because it gives us a case where correctness can be separated cleanly; a proof can be verified by AI without any human understanding how it works. What mathematicians still want after verification is a clue to what mechanical objectivity can’t provide.
Truth as a value-driven practice
Philosophers of science now predominantly reject the value-free ideal as being appropriate or helpful. Values enter because whether we reject or accept hypotheses is contingent on how we weigh consequences. Even in abstract realms like math, there are often simply too many possible truths for values not to be brought to bear in sifting through them. Mathematicians accepted long ago that in principle a machine can enumerate the set of theorems that can be proved from a given set of axioms. Yet the scale of this space is immense, motivating people to seek clever shortcuts for exploring it.
But even with automated theorem-proving at scale, not all theorems are equally interesting to people. Values are inherent in the choices that lead to certain open problems gaining widespread appeal, and in the processes by which the community comes to accept and internalize the results. Fermat’s Last Theorem initially got attention not because it was an inherently important conjecture, but because Fermat claimed to have a proof but never provided it, enticing others to try their hand. It became central when it was shown that it would follow from the modularity conjecture, which proposed a previously unanticipated link between disparate areas of math. It was considered solved after peer review exposed an error that led to a corrected version of the original proof, even though formal verification didn’t come until recently. Epistemic taste develops because without it, we face an undifferentiated flood of facts. Taste is a capacity we develop over time as we choose problems, pursue some of them, and see which yield new understanding or ideas.
If AI takes over choosing, we risk losing the personal fulfillment and community cooperation that motivates many to want to develop a capacity for scientific judgment in the first place. Tao makes a similar point by framing open problems as lighthouses rather than destinations. Reaching them prematurely with AI may sterilize the field around them. If, as fields are transformed by AI, we stop producing people who can judge what’s interesting and aligned with human aspirations, we may end up with a science that fails to serve basic human interests. Its results will consume attention from those to whom it is targeted, while providing neither fodder for subsequent discoveries nor contributing to the processes that help shape the next generation.
This starts to sound like motivation for a new kind of linear model for science, which ensures that human reflection and inquiry are sustained despite AI becoming better than the average mathematician. The risk of proceeding without human intervention is drift, as anyone who relies heavily on agents to carry out their work knows. Even when you think you’re providing a well-specified pipeline for implementing and verifying an idea, it’s easy to end up mired in nuance in some branch you never expected to traverse. When you don’t assert epistemic agency, you can easily end up with a “view from nowhere” – not a form of pure objectivity, but an answer without a corresponding question. Maintaining alignment is not a problem you solve once and move on from. It requires a supply of humans who can articulate and adjudicate between values.
Mechanical objectivity attempted to replace trust in individuals with trust in procedures, but that substitution has never happened as intended. To understand why, we need to look at the interactions that truth-seeking depends on.
Sociality is not contamination of rationality
There’s a tendency to see the social aspects of science as opposed to rationality. The social side of science can produce pathologies, like bad conventions, herd behavior, or deference to prestige. But scientific knowledge as we know it has always been the product of many epistemic agents bringing values and expertise to bear, and revising their views in response to challenge, not from some external verifying engine.
As the philosopher Helen Longino argues, the basis for objective public knowledge is a shared language and a belief that things we describe exist independently of how we perceive them. If we can agree on descriptions of the world, then two things become possible: we can defer to others’ experiences to obtain knowledge, and meaningfully criticize scientific claims.
Scientific communities develop shared standards and vocabulary that allow us to build on one another’s findings. We don’t need to verify everything firsthand, and sometimes relying on others’ findings can give us better grounds for believing something than investigating it ourselves, particularly when they possess evidence or expertise that we lack.
Without criticism, we cannot have objectivity; it is, as Longino puts it “dependent upon the depth and scope of the transformative interrogation that occurs in any given scientific community.” For criticism to be transformative requires someone who is obliged to take it up.
Practices like peer review and post-publication critique are not just fact-checks for sifting out false positives – they are about members of the community holding one another to the commitments that their assertions imply, and negotiating where to draw the line on the influence of personal preference. As Longino explains, “[t]he function of peer review is not just to check that the data seem right and the conclusions well-reasoned, but to bring to bear another point of view on the phenomena, whose expression might lead the original author(s) to revise the way they think about and present their observations and conclusions.”
Method itself is best understood as a social process, where progress depends on how well a community sustains critical dialogue. This dialogue builds the people in it, shaping what it means for them to understand and exercise judgment along with the knowledge it produces.
If criticism and an ability to trust others’ assertions are integral to the production of knowledge, we might ask whether AI can fulfill these same functions. Can models realize transformative criticism without human involvement? Can we trust the assertions of AI agents without obtaining direct understanding ourselves? And if we do, what happens to our own capacity to question, criticize, and stand behind results?
What does it mean to assert something is true?
The view that it shouldn’t matter who asserted some result as long as it’s correct corresponds to reliabilist epistemologies in philosophy. Classical epistemology insisted that true beliefs are only knowledge if the believer is able to produce reasons for their belief. In contrast, reliabilist epistemologies argue that true beliefs can, at least in some cases, represent genuine knowledge even when the believer can’t produce justifying reasons, provided they arrived at those beliefs by exercising capacities that are reliable producers of true beliefs in those circumstances.
But there are limits to what reliability can provide. The philosopher Robert Brandom imagines a community where the members hold true beliefs, which they have acquired through reliable means, but cannot offer reasons for any of them. Because attributing reliability to the source of their beliefs would itself provide a form of justification based on inference, the community can’t know that they are reliable. They are reliable as instruments indicating something about their surroundings, but unable to recognize themselves as such. Unable to even possess the concept of reliability, Brandom concludes, they cannot have knowledge.
If reliability alone can’t produce knowledge, what can? Brandom’s response is that calling something knowledge is a social act. To call what someone has “knowledge,” we have to attribute to them a commitment (that they believe that thing) along with an entitlement to that belief (that it is justified). But we also have to undertake that commitment ourselves, in the sense that we endorse the belief.
The scientist who first asserted the claim allows us to repeat the claim (and draw conclusions from it) while leaving them responsible for justifying it if challenged. We do this relatively easily in human science because if it turns out there was something wrong with the original assertion, there is an answerable source we can consult to resolve it. Assertions have social significance because we can hold the original author accountable for what was said. This is the sense of understanding that matters most for science, that mathematicians want after the proof has been verified, and that Tao’s patient wants too: results that can be interrogated and reconceptualized where needed, to avoid the perception of progress that fails to serve our goals.
But when we rely on AI results we don’t understand, there is only the person whose name is on the result to turn to. This is the problem arXiv is concerned with: no author can take responsibility for what they cannot understand, and hence they cannot respond to criticism by saying what it rests on, or whether it should be withdrawn. In other words, formal authorship survives while substantive authorship weakens. And so we lose the potential for transformative criticism, which is what sustains our notions of “objective” results in the first place.
Could AI act as an accountable epistemic agent?
A natural question is whether we could put the criticism to the AI agent itself, letting it decide whether to defend the result or concede and revise. What would it mean for AI to be an epistemic agent capable of committing to its assertions?
There are a few challenges with today’s agents that would need to be overcome. One is their lack of persistence and identity in the sense that we attribute it to people. An agent that retracts something it asserted in one session is not bound to maintain its correction or the reasoning behind it in the next. If each new result is produced by a new bespoke multi-agent infrastructure, it becomes hard to “keep score” in the way that naturally happens within networks of human scientists.
Scientific knowledge production depends on epistemic agents who have something at stake. Making bad claims changes the scientist’s standing in the community, which is how trust in individuals can remain calibrated. It’s not clear what comparable loss an AI agent faces in retracting its assertions, particularly given its lack of persistence.
To overcome such limitations would require a considerable shift in how we develop AI: away from being maximally helpful in each exchange and toward being accountable across them, as human scientists tend to be. This may well be possible. But I don’t think accountable AI will be enough to sustain meaningful science from our human perspective.
Let’s say we succeed in developing agents that can answer for claims. This is half of what accountability demands, but we also need others capable of holding them accountable, by asking for evidence, questioning assumptions, recognizing when an answer is evasive. Endorsements of others’ assertions are only as good as our capacity to engage with what we are endorsing.
These are capacities that get built by exercising them, by choosing problems, defending our work, reviewing papers, challenging others’ results. When we don’t exercise our capacities, we lose them. It’s not clear what we gain from a perfectly accountable AI if no one can judge how good its answers are. We’d have truth-seeking in theory, but no one who is able to do it.
Thurston’s notion of mathematical success points to this shared capacity to interrogate, extend, and repair a field’s knowledge that he’s hinting at. As he puts it, “As long as people in the field are comfortable that the idea works, it doesn’t need to have a formal written source.” Verification can tell us a result checks out in a technical sense, but only a community of people prepared to stand behind it can turn it into knowledge.
If we continue to appeal to value-free ideals that frame correctness as all that matters, we will keep building tools that prioritize answers while neglecting the truth-seeking and understanding of the people who can make them count.

results.summary:
The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into scientific research risks prioritizing verified outputs over human understanding, potentially undermining the critical accountability and social processes that sustain scientific knowledge.

### Key Points
- Northwestern University professor Jessica Hullman argues that scientific progress requires human judgment, not just the automated verification of results.
- The "value-free ideal" incorrectly suggests that scientific truth is purely procedural and independent of ethical or social context.
- Mathematician Terry Tao and others warn that relying on AI-generated solutions without human comprehension creates risks if the underlying logic is flawed.
- Scientific knowledge relies on transformative criticism, where researchers hold one another accountable for claims and methodologies.
- Current AI models lack the persistence and identity required to act as truly accountable epistemic agents within the scientific community.

### Why it Matters
Treating scientific truth as a collection of verified facts rather than a social, value-driven practice threatens to erode the human expertise necessary to interpret and build upon new discoveries. If researchers lose the ability to critically engage with AI outputs, the scientific community risks losing the capacity to distinguish between meaningful knowledge and mere data.

results.title: How the tiny soybean took over the American diet
results.author: Rachel Feltman, Alli Rodgers, Sushmita Pathak, Alex Sugiura
results.content:
Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
When you think about soy, what comes to mind? Maybe some salty edamame or a crispy chunk of fried tofu? But soybeans are actually kind of everywhere, from the oil most of your food is cooked in to the fuel that powers many of our vehicles. These days, almost half a billion metric tons of soybeans are grown globally in a year.
Environmental historian Edward Melillo recently wrote about how this humble legume quietly became one of the world’s most important crops—and why it’s almost impossible to avoid. He’s here to give us the inside scoop on soybean’s meteoric rise.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thanks so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Edward Melillo: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So I would love to start with just a little bit about what it means to be an environmental historian. It sounds like such an interesting field to be in.
Melillo: Sure, sure. So it’s a fascinating field, and I come by it very honestly. My dad is an ecologist, and my mom is a historian. And so I intertwine two limbs of the family tree and get paid to do it, which is a joy. And I study the way people understand and interact with nature in the past, and I mostly do that in the context of the Pacific world, the countries and cultures in and around the Pacific Ocean. I’ve spent a lot of time there, and I very much enjoy thinking about the, sort of, interactions in the past.
Feltman: So you wrote an article for the Conversationcalled “How Soybeans Took Over the American Diet—Without Anyone Noticing.” So let’s start with some context. How big a part of the American diet are soybeans?
Melillo: They’re extremely big. I mean, the soybean has become ubiquitous in the American diet. Sixty percent of processed foods contain some form of soy. And the numbers are really staggering; 2026 is on track to become a record soybean harvest for the U.S. It’s 4.52 billion bushels of soybeans to be harvested this year. And I did the math, and that adds up to about 800 pounds of soybeans per American. We’re not consuming all that as, sort of, soybeans on a plate because it becomes animal feed—it’s a product, as I said, that’s in all sorts of foods—and then it’s increasingly becoming a source of feedstock for biodiesel.
And so trucks and buses and commercial airplanes and passenger airplanes and, in addition, some cars are being powered by soy oil. And so soy is everywhere, at all times, and we hardly notice it, but you kinda can’t turn one way or the other without seeing something that’s got soy in it.
Feltman: A lot of our listeners, when they think of soybeans, they think of tofu. Where else is soy actually showing up?
Melillo: Oh, it’s, it’s absolutely everywhere. I mean, it’s in chocolate, in mayonnaise, in baby formula. And almost all the frying oil that’s used these days in the U.S. has soy oil in it. And I came to know this actually because my wife is allergic to soybeans. And there are about 1.5 million Americans who have a soy allergy, and most people don’t really think about that.
We go to restaurants, and folks will say, “Oh, we’ve got gluten-free alternatives.” And she’ll say, “Well, gluten isn’t the problem here at all. I love, love gluten in my bread, but it’s soy.” And, that’s led us down the road of, kind of, looking on menus and asking at restaurants. And as we’ve eaten, we’ve learned that soy is absolutely everywhere. It’s often used as an emulsifier to keep fats and solids from separating, and that’s in all sorts of products.
Feltman: Well, let’s talk a little bit about the history of the soybean. You know, where did it come from, and how was it first used in America?
Melillo: So the soybean—and its scientific name is Glycine max—was domesticated somewhere between 6,000 and 9,000 years ago in China. But it wasn’t until about 1764 when a sailor named Samuel Bowen, who had been spending time in China, brought some of these back as a souvenir to Savannah, Georgia. And he planted them, and they grew with reckless abandon. There were three or four harvests that first year, when they were planted on the surveyor-general’s farm in Savannah. And after that, Bowen tried to make a soy sauce from these soybeans, something similar to what he had seen in China. He died shortly thereafter, and the soybean kind of fell into unuse after that for a while.
But then, at the turn of the century, at about 1900, the U.S. agricultural experiment stations throughout the country began experimenting with soybeans as a possible animal feed. And that’s how the early history of the soybean kind of takes off, mostly being fed to animals. But then, in the 1930s, Henry Ford began a long-standing romance with the soybean. He became enamored of its possibilities as an industrial ingredient.
Melillo: And his vision really was that it would be a kind of vegetable steel, where American farmers could grow this crop that Ford could then use in his car factories as a basis for making paints and plastics and all sorts of other car components.
And by 1935 or so, it’s estimated that Ford was using about a bushel of soybeans in every car coming off of his factory line. So Ford not only was interested in using the soybean to make cars, but he also thought the soybean was the future of food.
And he had some discontents with that theory. Some of the people working for him didn’t so much appreciate some of the, the, the soy baked goods that he was producing. But, uh, that did not deter Ford. And in 1934, at the Chicago’s Century of Progress Exposition, reporters showed up and were treated to a banquet where every single food item was soy-based. There were soy biscuits and soy cheese and soy coffee and even an apple pie made with a soybean crust.
Feltman: “Protein maxxing” at the World’s Fair.
Melillo: [Laughs]. Right. Right. Uh, the reporters were kind of shocked, but some of them predicted, “Well, this may be the future of food.” And so Ford, sort of, carried that vision on.
And it is worth pointing out the dark side of the story because Ford, unfortunately, was a virulent antisemite. And in The Dearborn Independent, he published these antisemitic rants, and he actually received honors fr†om the Nazi government. And so Ford is a, sort of, contradictory figure in the whole story, but he certainly helped shape where, where soy began to enter U.S. markets in, in all these different ways. And things then sort of carried on into the postwar era in some different directions.
Feltman: Yeah, no, I’d, I’d love to hear about how soy went from being, you know, this kind of alien food ingredient, you know, that reporters were being presented with to being so ubiquitous in processed food.
Melillo: Yeah, so during the Second World War, the U.S. had been importing a lot of oil from Southeast Asia and other places that kind of went offline. And so, given these shortages, food producers started to turn to soybean oil as an alternative, and they learned that you could hydrogenate the oil by adding hydrogen to it and make it into a solid. And that solid provided the basis for margarine. And so, you know, during and after the Second World War, the rise of margarine is one of the food stories of U.S. history. Margarine begins to displace butter as one of the solids that Americans are consuming. And then, from there on, it’s just sort of a story of soy entering the U.S. diet from all sorts of different directions.
Producers figured out that you could use a chemical called n-hexane to get the oil and the solids out of soybeans, and you can feed the solids to animals—cows, pigs and chickens—and then you can use the oil in food production. And that oil began to enter all sorts of products, you know, and today we have an economy that’s, that really is driven by soy, and we hardly know it. It’s kind of all around us.
Feltman: And the ubiquitousness of soy is sometimes pretty controversial. Could you talk a little bit about, you know, the downsides or even just, you know, culturally perceived downsides of all this soy?
Melillo: Well, one of the tricks is that soybeans are heavily genetically modified. Ninety-seven percent of soybeans are. And the reason for that is that it makes the soybean herbicide tolerant. But then, of course, when the soybean is processed, all those herbicides and other chemicals stay in the soybean. And so one of the questions is: We’re consuming all this soy. What else are we consuming in the process? And that’s controversial, and there’s a lot of scholarship on both sides of that. But that is certainly an issue.
The other’s just: If you’ve got a soybean allergy, it’s really hard to tell that soy’s in the food you’re eating. ’Cause when you go out to a restaurant and stuff is fried, it’s fried in vegetable oil, but that’s one of the terms under which soy masquerades. And vegetable oil often contains soy oil. You don’t know if it’s canola oil or some other vegetable oil, but it often has soybean oil. So it’s also just hard to tell where it’s lurking in your diet.
The thing about soy is its versatility. As I said, it shows up in animal feed, in fuel. It’s an emulsifier. It’s in frying oil. And so it gets involved in all sorts of things like trade wars. China’s now the world’s leading consumer of soybean meal, the solids that come from soy—and that’s because China’s trying to feed 1.4 billion people, and a lot of the soy’s going into animal feed.
And one of the principal exporters to China is the U.S., so these trade wars that have been going on with Trump and China have often been soy-centered. China had slapped 25 percent tariffs on soy imports at one point, and now those tariffs are lowered, and so U.S. farmers can begin exporting soybeans to China again.
But the other big issue is that Brazil is one of the other leading producers of soybeans. And soy farming is one of the leading causes of deforestation in the southwestern Amazon. And so, in states like Mato Grosso, you see huge swaths of forest being cut down to create soybean plantations to grow soy for animal feed export.
And we can start to see the cascades of problems that might arise from those patterns. And so soy gets implicated in all sorts of things, from deforestation to trade wars, in ways that you wouldn’t have expected and and couldn’t have even anticipated when you were in Henry Ford’s kitchen in the 1930s.
Feltman: I guess one last question I have is just that, you know, being such a versatile crop that has now gotten into so many industries, so many products, what do efforts to replace soy look like? You know, if we’re talking about areas where people are concerned about deforestation or, you know, concerned about pesticide contamination, what crops do we see stepping up to take some of the soybeans off of our plate?
Melillo: There’s not a lot at the moment. I mean, soy is just going gangbusters, and it’s closed in on corn as, as the leading crop grown in the U.S. several times. In 2018, in fact, soy surpassed corn. And the world seems to be turning to soy in more ways than one. Europe is still a holdout. You can travel fairly extensively throughout Europe and not encounter this, sort of, ubiquitous soy. They use canola oil, rapeseed oil, for some of the same purposes. But throughout much of the world, it’s a soy-hungry world, and soy is doing really well. If you were to think of this as a plant success story, this is nearing the apex for soy. And so that’s one way to think about this.
Feltman: Well, you know, I know this is maybe gonna come more from personal experience than from your scholarly work, but what advice do you have for people who do need to try to avoid soy and are, you know, kind of, newly confronted with, uh, how it’s everywhere?
Melillo: You have to read ingredient lists carefully and be really direct in restaurants because often your servers, uh, and even the people cooking in, in those restaurants won’t know that soy is there. And so you have to ask them to read the label on the cooking oil. And it just takes a lot of effort to figure this puzzle out because, as I said, it’s sort of everywhere.
Michael Pollan, who writes a lot about plants, had suggested, at one point, that you go to a gas station, and you’re putting corn into your body and corn into your car, ’cause there’s corn syrup in everything on the shelves at the gas station, and there’s corn ethanol in the fuel. But that’s now becoming true, as well, of soy, where soy is absolutely everywhere in the food we’re eating, but it’s also because of, you know, these federal, renewable fuel mandates have put soy at the top of the list as an ingredient that can go into creating biodiesel. And so we’re seeing the same thing happening that happened with corn with soy for sure, where it just is everywhere at all times, but yet it’s quite invisible.
Feltman: Hmm. Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Melillo: Thank you so much for having me. It was a real pleasure to talk with you.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to talk about another commodity that’s taken the nation by storm with surprising speed: artificial intelligence.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Sushmita Pathak, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, this is Rachel Feltman. See you next time!

Soybeans have become a ubiquitous global commodity, integrated into 60 percent of processed American foods, animal feed, and biodiesel, despite remaining largely invisible to the average consumer.

### Key Points
- The U.S. is projected to harvest a record 4.52 billion bushels of soybeans in 2026, averaging roughly 800 pounds per American.
- Originally domesticated in China, the crop was introduced to the U.S. in 1764 by sailor Samuel Bowen before being popularized industrially by Henry Ford in the 1930s.
- Approximately 97 percent of U.S. soybeans are genetically modified for herbicide tolerance, raising concerns about chemical residues in food products.
- Soy production is a significant driver of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon and a frequent focal point in international trade disputes, particularly with China.

The extreme versatility of the soybean has made it a cornerstone of the modern global economy, linking food security, industrial fuel production, and environmental health. Because the crop is so deeply embedded in supply chains, its widespread use creates significant challenges for allergy sufferers and complicates efforts to address the ecological impacts of large-scale industrial agriculture.
