results.title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
results.author: Phil Muncaster
results.content:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.
Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.
“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.
“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”
The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.
An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.
The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.
“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”
According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.
The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations
On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.
The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.
Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.
After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.
“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.
Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.
Clean-Up Time
Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.
It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.
The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.
Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.
“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.
“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."
results.summary:
Binance revealed that a sophisticated, months-long social engineering campaign targeting its software engineers resulted in a massive digital heist involving XRP, SOL, and OP cryptocurrency assets.

### Key Points
- Attackers used fake recruitment interviews and malicious code repositories to compromise the work computer of a Binance software engineer in September.
- The breach utilized zero-day malware designed to evade endpoint security tools by replacing legitimate development components with malicious versions.
- Hackers gained access to internal AI tools and stolen credentials to compromise additional employees, including Wallet DevOps and Software engineers.
- On October 29, attackers triggered malicious scripts to drain 233.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL, and 44.2 million OP from Binance hot wallets.
- Binance has since rebuilt its wallet systems, decommissioned compromised credentials, and enhanced behavioral anomaly detection to prevent future unauthorized access.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the severe risks posed by targeted social engineering against high-privilege employees, even within organizations with established security protocols. It underscores the critical need for companies to balance developer productivity with strict controls over software execution and internal access permissions.

results.title: Tech Odyssey Series: From Portugal to China, a New Conversation Begins
results.author: TechNode Staff
results.content:
In the previous episode of Tech Odyssey, we visited Startup Braga to see how a former police building became a startup hub with global ambitions. For the season finale, we speak with AICEP, Portugal’s trade and investment agency and the series’ co-producer, about what might come next for technology cooperation between Portugal and China.
“Have you been to Portugal?”
A friend from Singapore put that question to Dr. Gang Lu, Founder and CEO of TechNode Group and Co-founder of BEYOND, during a chance encounter in Thailand, two weeks before the recording of the Tech Odyssey season finale.
He had watched the series. Now, he was seriously considering expanding his business into Portugal.
It was an unexpected connection: a programme exploring Portugal’s technology sector had reached someone elsewhere in Asia and prompted him to look at a market he might otherwise have overlooked.
That was part of what AICEP hoped to achieve through the series. For Luís Costa, director of AICEP Shanghai and Portugal’s Economic and Commercial Counsellor in China, the exchange also worked in the other direction. The Portuguese founders featured in the programme had an opportunity to learn more about China.
“We are bringing China to them,” Costa said, “and hopefully they’ll eventually consider China when they go overseas.”
Helping Companies Find Their Next Market
AICEP is Portugal’s public trade and investment agency, operating under the Ministry of Economy. Its work runs in two directions: helping Portuguese companies expand internationally and attracting foreign investment into Portugal.
For Costa’s team in China, that means supporting Portuguese businesses exploring the Chinese market while engaging with Chinese companies interested in investing or producing in Portugal.
There is also a broader task: building confidence.
Costa wants prospective investors and buyers to see Portugal as a reliable country to do business with. Making that case requires more than a national introduction. Companies need people who understand the market they are entering.
Francisco Catalão, a former member of AICEP’s board, described an overseas network spanning more than 50 markets, with teams of different sizes depending on local needs and existing business ties.
Those representatives serve as local points of contact for Portuguese companies. A business considering Shanghai, for example, can turn to Costa and his team for knowledge of the commercial environment and help making connections.
For Catalão, that local expertise is central to the network’s value. A company may have a product ready for export, but finding the right partners and understanding how a new market operates require a different kind of preparation.
A Broader Picture of Portugal
Portugal’s wine, food and traditional industries are familiar to international audiences. Its technology companies are often less visible.
Costa saw Tech Odyssey as an opportunity to broaden that picture: to show founders developing new products, universities supporting emerging businesses, and institutions helping ideas reach the market.
One characteristic stood out throughout the series: Portuguese startups tend to think internationally early in their development.
Costa described founders considering overseas customers, partners and sources of capital almost from the outset. International expansion becomes part of how they build the company, rather than a decision reserved for a later stage.
Catalão placed those businesses within a wider economy that combines established export industries with newer areas of research and development. Alongside agriculture, wine and food, he highlighted pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and the blue economy, including technologies linked to the ocean.
Across the season, that range became tangible through visits to companies working on spatial audio, smart urban infrastructure, rehabilitation equipment and environmental monitoring. Together, they offered a more detailed view of what Portuguese technology businesses are building—and where they hope to sell it.
Where Could Portugal and China Work Together?
Asked which sectors Chinese companies should look at more closely, Costa pointed first to medical and health technology.
In his view, the potential for partnerships and investment in those fields deserves greater attention. He highlighted Portugal’s engineers, university network and research capabilities, along with incentives available to companies willing to invest and produce in the country.
“Personally, I see health tech as a big opportunity” for Chinese companies, he said.
The conversation also turned to hardware. China’s capabilities in hardware development and manufacturing were familiar territory for Lu. What surprised him during the trip was the number of Portuguese businesses working on physical products and related technologies.
Costa agreed that there was scope to explore partnerships. The pace of business in Portugal may differ from that in cities such as Shenzhen, but companies can still find shared commercial interests.
That is where AICEP’s role becomes practical: helping businesses identify potential partners and develop those initial conversations.
Making the Case for Portugal
For a Chinese company considering production in Europe, the decision involves several questions at once: access to talent, location, logistics, energy, operating conditions and the economics of the investment.
Costa pointed to Portugal’s connections with other European markets and its Atlantic-facing position in relation to the Americas and Africa. He also highlighted the country’s high share of renewable electricity generation.
Portugal’s openness to foreign investment was another part of his pitch.
“We want more Chinese companies to continue investing in Portugal and making partnerships with Portuguese companies,” he said.
In discussions with Chinese investors, Costa finds that many of the factors AICEP presents match what businesses are looking for: a smooth process, ease of doing business and a workable balance of costs and returns.
Those considerations give companies reasons to investigate further. Whether a particular project makes sense will ultimately depend on its own requirements, partners and commercial case.
From One Article to a Full Season
The idea behind this season began on a much smaller scale.
Costa recalled a first meeting three years earlier, when the discussion centred on a single article introducing Portugal. AICEP would provide material, and TechNode would select the stories most relevant to its audience.
That proposal eventually became a web series built around four days of visits to Portuguese cities, universities, incubators, investors and technology companies.
For Costa, the resulting programmes have value beyond their initial release. Available on platforms including Bilibili, YouTube and LinkedIn, they create a record that future audiences can return to when looking for an introduction to Portugal’s innovation ecosystem.
The encounter in Thailand offered one small indication of how those stories might travel. A viewer in Singapore had watched the programme and begun considering Portugal as a place to expand his business.
Costa hopes Portuguese founders will make a similar discovery in the other direction—that seeing and hearing from China will encourage them to consider a market outside their existing plans.
The season ends with that possibility still open. The visits are over, but the companies, technologies and people encountered along the way give viewers somewhere concrete to begin their next conversation.
results.summary:
The Tech Odyssey web series, produced by AICEP, highlights Portugal’s growing technology sector to foster international business partnerships and investment opportunities between Portuguese companies and the Chinese market.

### Key Points
- AICEP, Portugal’s trade and investment agency, produced the Tech Odyssey series to showcase the country's innovation ecosystem to global audiences.
- The series highlights diverse sectors including health technology, biotechnology, spatial audio, and the blue economy.
- Luís Costa, director of AICEP Shanghai, emphasizes Portugal's appeal through its renewable energy, strategic location, and openness to foreign investment.
- The program aims to facilitate two-way growth by helping Portuguese startups expand into China while attracting Chinese companies to invest in Portugal.
- The series is available on platforms like YouTube, LinkedIn, and Bilibili to serve as a long-term resource for international business development.

### Why it Matters
This initiative demonstrates how digital media can effectively bridge geographical gaps to stimulate cross-border economic cooperation and foreign direct investment. By highlighting specific industrial strengths, AICEP provides a practical framework for companies to evaluate new markets and establish strategic international partnerships.

results.title: Democrats in House Poised to Investigate the Trump Administration
results.author: Yves Smith
results.content:
Yves here. The Democrats and their pundit allies, as Democrat midterm prospects brightened, talked up investigations as a key way to bring the hyper-aggressive, rule-and-law ignoring Administration to heel. As of the time of this post, the Democrats had not yet officially cinched the House, but that has been widely expected, and with the Democrats seizing the Senate, a House majority looks more likely.
There are some nuances here. A big Democratic margin in the House would actually give the progressive wing less power, since their votes would be less essential in passing resolutions and legislation.
The article goes through some highs and lows of past efforts to investigate controversies and alleged crime. The piece acknowledges that the Executive branch can stonewall. It does not point out that Congress can impeach member of the Administration, but how far this can go is an untested question. From Congress.gov:
Article II, Section 4:
The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors….
Historical practice thus informs the understanding of who qualifies as a civil officer. Aside from the President and Vice President, who are plainly identified in the Constitution’s text as impeachable officials, historical practice indicates that federal judges clearly qualify as officers subject to impeachment and removal, as the majority of proceedings have applied to those positions.6 Congress has also impeached the head of a cabinet-level Executive department.7 While this indicates a congressional understanding that high-level Executive officers may be subject to impeachment, it is unclear how far down the ranks of the federal bureaucracy this principle travels.
Now to the main event.
By Drew Kurlowski, Associate Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University and Gibbs Knotts, Professor of Political Science, Coastal Carolina University. Originally published at The Conversation
Oversight is coming for the Trump administration.
That’s been the message of congressional Democrats throughout the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign. Now that the party’s candidates have reportedly won control of the House of Representatives, that campaign promise is likely to be carried out. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told The New York Times in late October that among the potential oversight targets were pardons granted by President Donald Trump, possible corruption in government contracting and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency deals.
Routine congressional oversight hearings usually don’t make headlines.
That changed during the second Trump administration.
When Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, what took place was a contentious, highly partisan, made-for-TV-and-social-media confrontation.
Bondi refused to answer many questions from Democrats, instead launching personal attacks against these members of the U.S. Senate.
The episode captures a basic tension in congressional oversight: Congress can demand answers, but getting them often depends on the cooperation of the branch it is investigating.
That tension is about to sharpen when Democrats control the oversight process. Their hearings will likely be anything but routine.
From our perspective as political scientists who study the U.S. Congress, congressional oversight has played an important role in American democracy. Here’s a brief history.
Inquisitory Powers
In simple terms, oversight is the ability of Congress to ensure that the laws it passes are faithfully executed. This generally means asking questions, demanding information, convening hearings and holding the executive branch accountable for its actions.
Oversight isn’t specifically mentioned in the Constitution. Article 1, Section 8, which lists the powers of Congress, includes the power “to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper,” without identifying an oversight role. Once laws are enacted, Article 2, Section 3, states that the president “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.”
However, the framers viewed congressional oversight as a key component of legislative authority. They wanted presidents to take Congress seriously and structured the Constitution to ensure that the executive would be accountable to the legislature.
As James Madison urged in Federalist 51, the separate branches of government should have the power to keep each other from becoming too powerful. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” Madison wrote.
The framers drew from the examples of the British Parliament and Colonial legislatures. In 1621, Sir Francis Bacon was charged with corruption and impeached as Lord High Chancellor after an investigation by a committee of the British Parliament. And in 1768, the Massachusetts Assembly conducted an investigation of Gov. Francis Bernard that led to a formal request to the King of England for his removal.
At the Federal Convention in 1787 that produced the Constitution, Delegate George Mason noted that members of Congress possessed “inquisitory powers” and “must meet frequently to inspect the Conduct of public officials.” Even though this idea was never written down, it was a habit of self-government that early Congresses put into practice.
Early Oversight Hearings
Congressional oversight began almost as soon as the first Congress met. In 1790, Robert Morris, the superintendent of finances during the Continental Congress and a financier of the American Revolution, asked Congress to investigate his handling of the country’s finances and was exonerated of any wrongdoing.
During this period, congressional investigations were often referred to select committees – bodies created to perform special functions. These panels had the power to issue subpoenas and hold individuals in contempt. Since there was no official record of debates and proceedings, the public relied on newspaper accounts to learn about what had happened.
In March 1792, congressional oversight exposed businessman William Duer, who signed contracts with the War Department but failed to furnish the needed military supplies. This shortfall contributed to a stunning U.S. military defeat against a confederation of Native American tribes in the Northwest Territory.
Congress eventually removed the quartermaster general from his role for mismanaging the contracts.
Throughout the 19th century, Congress continued to quietly exercise this power.
Hearings from December 1861 to May 1865 on the conduct of the U.S. Civil War produced a detailed record of the war, exposed military wrongdoing and condemned slavery. In 1871, the Senate created a select committee to investigate Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction.
Investigating Corruption and Criminal Acts
Congress started to use its oversight power more aggressively in the 1920s with the Senate Committee on Public Land and Surveys’ high-profile investigations into the Teapot Dome scandal.
Hearings revealed that Interior Secretary Albert Bacon Fall had secretly leased federal oil reserves in Wyoming to two private corporations and had received personal loans and gifts from the companies in return.
The investigation found clear evidence of corruption. Fall was indicted and became the first U.S. Cabinet member to be convicted of a felony.
The U.S. Supreme Court helped to shape the legal foundation of congressional oversight. In McGrain v. Daugherty, decided in 1927, the court held that congressional committees could issue subpoenas, force witnesses to testify and hold them in contempt if they fail to appear. Two years later, in Sinclair v. United States, the court ruled that witnesses who lied to Congress could be charged with perjury.
These cases granted the judicial branch’s sanction to what had long been an implied legislative power, cementing the constitutionality of congressional oversight.
Oversight Highs and Lows
The modern era of congressional oversight has produced some very important reforms – and some truly regrettable spectacles.
The most important example of bipartisan congressional oversight came in response to reporting by The Washington Post’s Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The two journalists wrote about the 1972 burgling of Democratic National Committee offices in Washington, D.C.’s Watergate Hotel and subsequent cover-up efforts by the Nixon administration – and President Richard Nixon himself.
On Feb. 7, 1973, the U.S. Senate voted 77-0 to establish a Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities, which brought together Democrats and Republicans to investigate what came to be known as the “Watergate scandal.” The committee’s work spurred action in Congress to impeach Nixon, leading to Nixon’s resignation in 1974 and to the enactment of legal reforms to provide an institutional check on presidential power.
Another high point for congressional oversight came after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001. Seeking to learn how the deadliest terrorist strike on American soil had occurred, Democratic Sen. Bob Graham and Republican Rep. Porter Goss, who chaired the Senate and House Intelligence committees, formed a joint committee to investigate intelligence failures before and after the attacks.
This inquiry produced several important recommendations that were ultimately adopted, including the creation of a director of national intelligence and a Department of Homeland Security, as well as better information sharing among law enforcement agencies.
Congress’ oversight can extend beyond the executive branch when the actions of private actors raise questions about existing laws or spur the need for new ones. Investigations into medical device safety and Enron’s 2001 collapseexamined malfeasance in the private sphere that existing regulations failed to prevent.
However, the power to expose corruption can also be used as a tool to score partisan points and generate outrage, rather than holding the executive branch accountable for actual malfeasance. Notably, in the 1950s, Wisconsin Sen. Joseph McCarthy turned oversight into inquisition and used the power of media to amplify his accusations of communist influence within the federal government.
Democracy Needs Oversight
As we see it, the problem with allowing oversight to become political theater is that it distracts Congress from quieter and more meaningful oversight work. Slow, procedural work isn’t likely to go viral, but it helps keep government accountable. The task of a deliberate legislative body is to reconcile those very different impulses.
Congressional oversight has strengthened the democratic system at many points. But it can also be stymied by an uncooperative executive branch.
After the 2018 midterm elections put Democrats in charge of the House of Representatives, their many attempts to exercise oversight were rejected by the first Trump administration, which refused to send officials to testify at hearings, failed to turn over documents and ignored subpoenas.
Will the next two years of divided government look the same?
results.summary:
Following their reported victory in the House of Representatives, congressional Democrats are preparing to launch aggressive oversight investigations into the Trump administration’s policies and potential executive branch misconduct.

### Key Points
- Democrats plan to investigate specific targets, including presidential pardons, government contracting practices, and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency business dealings.
- Congressional oversight is an implied legislative power, supported by Supreme Court rulings like *McGrain v. Daugherty*, which affirmed the authority to issue subpoenas and hold witnesses in contempt.
- Historical oversight successes include the Watergate investigation, which led to President Richard Nixon’s resignation, and the post-9/11 inquiry that established the Department of Homeland Security.
- The effectiveness of these investigations remains uncertain, as the executive branch can stonewall requests by refusing to provide documents or blocking officials from testifying.
- Political scientists warn that oversight risks becoming partisan theater, which may distract from the essential, procedural work required to maintain government accountability.

### Why it Matters
Congressional oversight serves as a critical constitutional check on executive power, ensuring that laws are faithfully executed and government corruption is exposed. As Democrats assume control of the House, the resulting investigations will test the limits of legislative authority against an executive branch that has historically resisted such scrutiny.

results.title: This $40 smart home display promises up to two years of battery life
results.author: Hamed Paydarfar
results.content:
Summary
- The $39.90 OpenDisplay monochrome dashboard promises up to two years of battery life with updates every 15 minutes.
- The pricier $75.90 color model lasts about one year and is better suited to calendars, schedules, and other slowly changing information.
- Both models support Home Assistant and Bluetooth Low Energy, while arriving assembled with an enclosure, stand, battery, and preinstalled firmware.
Very recently, Seeed Studio launched a $39.90 e-paper smart home dashboard that, based on the company's claims, can run for up to two years between charges. According to the company’s announcement, the OpenDisplay 4.26-inch Mono Kit comes fully assembled with a rechargeable battery and native Home Assistant integration.
A larger 7.3-inch model with a color display is also available. It's priced at $75.90, and the battery life only lasts for about a year — yes, "only" a year. Both models can receive information over Bluetooth Low Energy and have built-in features for showing weather, calendar inputs, sensor readings, reminders, and other data without having to remain connected to a power outlet.
The cheaper OpenDisplay makes the better smart home dashboard
And that's especially true if you're into affordable DIY projects
The specs on both models are interesting. The smaller monochrome display packs an 800x400 e-paper panel with a Seeed XIAO EN05 board and a 2,000 mAh battery. Besides black and white, it can also take advantage of an optional four-level grayscale mode.
More often than not, a smart home dashboard is used to display information that doesn't need to be refreshed frequently. Thankfully, the e-paper display can do partial refreshes to preserve more battery. This is exactly how this display manages to get two years on a 2,000 mAh battery, but your phone display can barely last a full day of streaming with a battery that's double in size. Seeed bases its two-year estimate on the screen receiving an update every 15 minutes. The result will naturally vary based on the use case, but that update schedule is frequent enough for room temperatures, electricity usage, and other smart home data.
On the other hand, the $75.90 model has a one-year estimate that assumes one update every two hours. With that in mind, it's probably more suited to family calendars, daily schedules, or other such things that don't require rapidly changing sensor readings. In other words, spending more doesn't necessarily get you the more capable dashboard.
We recently covered a $25 kit that lets you build an e-paper dashboard for your desk, but OpenDisplay would be right up your alley if you'd rather skip most of the assembly. The included enclosure, stand, and firmware allow you to use it right out of the box (and after configuration with the rest of your smart home, of course).
results.summary:
Seeed Studio has launched the OpenDisplay e-paper smart home dashboard series, offering two pre-assembled models that provide long-lasting battery performance and native integration with Home Assistant platforms.

### Key Points
- The 4.26-inch monochrome model costs $39.90 and offers up to two years of battery life with 15-minute update intervals.
- The 7.3-inch color model is priced at $75.90 and provides approximately one year of battery life with two-hour update intervals.
- Both devices feature Bluetooth Low Energy connectivity and arrive fully assembled with an enclosure, stand, battery, and preinstalled firmware.
- The monochrome unit utilizes an 800x400 e-paper panel powered by a 2,000 mAh battery and a Seeed XIAO EN05 board.
- These displays support partial refreshes to optimize power consumption for data like weather, sensor readings, and calendar schedules.

### Why it Matters
- These low-power displays offer a practical, maintenance-free alternative to traditional tablets for monitoring smart home data without requiring constant power connections. By providing pre-assembled kits, Seeed Studio lowers the barrier to entry for users seeking to integrate e-paper technology into their home automation setups.

results.title: How Secure Is iCloud Keychain Compared To The Alternatives?
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Chifundo Kasiya)
results.content:
How Secure Is iCloud Keychain Compared To The Alternatives?
iCloud Keychain is a password manager built into iOS, iPadOS, and macOS. If you own an Apple device that supports these operating systems, you might wonder whether Keychain is secure compared to alternatives like Bitwarden, Proton Pass, and NordPass. It does everything a modern password manager does, including generating passwords and autofilling them. You can also use it to store passkeys and other sensitive information, such as credit cards and security codes. One of its biggest features is that it syncs this information between all your devices that use the same Apple account. You can then access your stored Keychain information through the Passwords app.
How secure is the iCloud Keychain? Very secure. It uses advanced encryption algorithms and end-to-end encryption (E2EE) when encrypting your data and syncing it between devices. Keychain also uses on-device authentication methods when autofilling information. Also, two-factor authentication (2FA) is a requirement when using iCloud Keychain with Apple accounts.
While Keychain doesn't offer the same security as Bitwarden or 1Password in every aspect, you can expect the fundamental protections that all reputable password managers swear by. There are some extra areas where it can improve when compared to its alternatives. However, those might not be deal breakers if you're primarily interested in everyday password security.
Why you can trust iCloud Keychain like its alternatives
Keychain uses AES-256 encryption, which is considered the gold standard and is used and recommended by the National Security Agency (NSA). This is the same encryption used by popular password managers like Bitwarden, 1Password, and Kaspersky Password Manager. Keychain doesn't store the decryption keys in iCloud, but locally on your device in its Secure Enclave. Although the Secure Enclave is integrated within the system-on-chip (SoC), it exists as its own isolated subsystem that remains secure even when the device's core systems become compromised. Information from the Secure Enclave can be accessed using Touch ID, Face ID, or the passcode.
Also, with E2EE, it means that your Keychain data is encrypted on your Apple device before being synced to iCloud. Not even Apple can read it because it doesn't have access to the keys. Even if someone were to hack your iCloud account or an Apple employee were to go rogue and leak it, no one can access your Keychain data since they also don't have the decryption keys.
iCloud Keychain also uses Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode when autofilling passwords and other information on websites and apps. For iPhones, you can enable Stolen Device Protection in Settings. It removes the passcode option for sensitive actions, like viewing Keychain passwords, when you're not in familiar locations like your home or office, leaving only the very secure biometric options that cannot be guessed or easily spoofed.
Keychain could improve in some areas
One area in which Keychain can do better is data breach monitoring. Keychain only scans for leaked passwords, while Bitwarden, Proton Pass, and NordPass can provide data breach reports telling you if your email or credit card information was exposed. Yes, even email exposure can open you up to significant risks, including spam and phishing attacks.
If someone knows your Apple device's passcode, they can access your passwords. Stolen device protection helps mitigate this somewhat, but if the person is in a familiar location, they can still use your passcode. Also, these biometrics can fail if the hardware develops a fault. Other password managers still use a master password, which creates an independent authentication method. Keep in mind that passwords are the weakest link in the security chain, which is why Microsoft removed the master password from Edge. But if you create an impossibly strong password and keep it safe, a master password can be incredibly secure.
Also, Keychain exports passwords as an unencrypted CSV. Anyone with access to your device can read the file. Bitwarden, for example, allows you to encrypt the exported backup. That option is only good for importing it into Bitwarden again, but if you want to export it elsewhere or keep it on your device, you can protect it with a password. It will still be encrypted, but entering the password will allow other password managers to decrypt it if they support the format.
results.summary:
iCloud Keychain provides robust security for Apple users through end-to-end encryption and hardware-based protection, though it lacks some advanced features found in dedicated third-party password management services.

### Key Points
- iCloud Keychain utilizes AES-256 encryption and stores decryption keys locally within the device's isolated Secure Enclave.
- Data is protected by end-to-end encryption, ensuring that Apple cannot access user passwords or sensitive information synced to iCloud.
- Authentication relies on biometric tools like Face ID and Touch ID, supplemented by mandatory two-factor authentication for Apple accounts.
- Stolen Device Protection adds security by requiring biometrics for sensitive actions when the device is away from familiar locations.
- Unlike competitors such as Bitwarden or NordPass, Keychain lacks comprehensive data breach monitoring for emails and credit cards.
- Keychain exports data as unencrypted CSV files, whereas some third-party managers allow users to password-protect exported backups.

### Why it Matters
Choosing between built-in tools and dedicated password managers involves balancing Apple's seamless ecosystem integration against the advanced security features offered by specialized software. While Keychain is highly secure for general users, those requiring cross-platform compatibility or enhanced breach reporting may prefer third-party alternatives.

Booking.com is positioning its platform as the primary destination for travelers to finalize reservations after using generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Gemini for initial trip planning.

results.title: A New Search Engine Lets You Explore 4 Million Works of Art & Historical Photographs from Museums and Libraries Around the World
results.author: Colin Marshall
results.content:
We live in an age when you can describe practically anything you want to see in words, then see it almost immediately. Nobody will ever have laid eyes upon that particular sight before — and quite possibly, nobody ever will again. There we have both the upside and the downside of artificial intelligence-powered image generation. A constant flow of visual, aural, or textual novelty offers stimulation, to put it mildly, but it inevitably comes to feel insubstantial. However complexly derived from the work of humanity it may be, it lacks a direct connection to that work. Not so the results delivered by Arkivism, a new search engine that responds to descriptions by drawing on a collection of more than four million pieces of real art and photography.
You may need a “town at sunset,” a “colorful cake,” a “rocket ship blasting off,” a “Japanese woodblock print of a cat,” or something else besides. Arkivism will more than likely be able to come up with more than a few images to fit the bill, with sources at hand including the Library of Congress, the NASA Video and Image Library, the Rijksmuseum, and Japan’s National Diet Library. (I notice that its reach extends even to the Gongu Copyright Commission in Korea, where I live, which will make it my go-to site when next I need to evoke the Joseon Dynasty.) The chance of discovering a work of art you’d never heard of is always high, even if you search a big name like Rembrandt, Leonardo, Klimt, or Hokusai.
“Every work indexed here is CC0 or public domain,” says Arkivism’s about page. “Download it, adapt it, use it in client work — no permission needed, no strings.” Like all the best online services, this one was designed to answer the actual needs of its creator, “a designer and video creator who kept needing imagery that was genuinely safe to use — and kept losing afternoons to a dozen museum search boxes.” Even if your work has nothing to do with design or video creation, you never know when you’ll be looking for a picture of a castle, a painting of a feast, or a map of the world. Sure, you could always ask AI to generate one for you, and you’d get something more or less usable. Sometimes that’s what you need; other times, you’re ready to be led down a historical and cultural rabbit hole. Enter Arkivism here.
via Kottke
Related content:
Based in Seoul, Colin Marshall writes and broadcasts on cities, language, and culture. He’s the author of the newsletter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Summarizing Korea) and Korean Newtro. Follow him on the social network formerly known as Twitter at @colinmarshall.
results.summary:
The new search engine Arkivism provides users with access to over four million public domain images sourced from major global institutions like NASA and the Rijksmuseum.

### Key Points
- Arkivism indexes more than four million pieces of real art and photography for public use.
- The platform sources content from reputable institutions including the Library of Congress, NASA, and the Rijksmuseum.
- All indexed works are classified as CC0 or public domain, allowing for free adaptation and commercial use without permission.
- The search engine was created by a designer to streamline the process of finding high-quality, legally safe imagery for creative projects.

### Why it Matters
Arkivism offers a reliable alternative to AI-generated imagery by providing authentic, historically significant visual assets that are free from copyright restrictions. This tool simplifies professional workflows for designers and creators while encouraging the discovery of genuine cultural and historical works.

results.title: What AI-generated malware looks like under the microscope
results.author: Mirko Zorz
results.content:
What AI-generated malware looks like under the microscope
In this Help Net Security interview, Lindsay Kaye, VP of Threat Intelligence at HUMAN Security, talks about what AI-generated malware looks like on the bench. She points to tidy comments, uniform logging messages, and emojis as signs a script came from a model, and notes that decompiled code strips much of that away. Kaye also covers how AI is squeezing the time teams have to patch, where it helps criminals scale fraud, and why her team keeps a human reviewing every conclusion before it goes out.
If you’re at Nullcon Berlin, Kaye is participating in the panel discussion “Agents Gone Wild” on November 5, 15:30–16:15.
You built your career taking malware apart by hand. When you reverse something you suspect was written with AI help, what looks different on the bench, and what looks exactly like it did five years ago?
As of right now, I have not explicitly reverse engineered malware written fully by AI in my current job – at least to my knowledge – which I’d consider something similar to the VoidLink malware disclosed by CheckPoint. Sometimes, I do come across scripts or pieces of code that look to be written using AI, and there are a few things that really stand out:
- In malicious scripts (so, NOT decompiled/disassembled code) you’ll see comments describing each function, often in the same type or format or sometimes with emojis. While this is certainly considered good practice in software development, this is not something a malware author would do. In decompiled code, as you know, comments would no longer be present, since they disappeared during compilation.
- Similarly, in decompiled/disassembled code, you might see logging messages that are all very similarly structured, with good spelling and grammar like you’d see in a professional codebase. You might also again see the use of emojis.
- In my current role, I focus extensively on advertising fraud which often materializes in mobile apps and HTML5 game sites. Before AI, we’d see tens of apps as part of campaigns but now, generating app content is so much easier that we see hundreds. Of course, now when we look at these apps/sites, they look mass-produced or share technical commonalities, and we see new ones emerge much more quickly than in the past.
While not EVERY piece of code that has these features is AI-generated, code generated using an LLM is “planned out” and will be structured according to “good” design patterns and coding behavior. However, when looking at decompiled/disassembled code itself (outside of the indicators I pointed out earlier), you do lose a lot of context, since decompilers can’t perfectly rebuild C/C++-like code. Add on obfuscation and it becomes even more challenging to discern. As for what has looked exactly the same, a few things I’ve continued to see are:
- Example code easily found on the internet still makes an appearance in malware. Whether this is copied by hand (as it was in the past) or surfaced using an LLM prompt, you’ll often see evidence such as use of “placeholder” names (such as “MyWindowClass”) that suggest the code was not generated by the author.
- We still see people use obfuscation toolkits, such as O-MVLL, or custom techniques to make code harder to reverse engineer. Both these toolkits and the custom techniques can be pretty advanced, and make analysis very challenging; however, now, discerning whether a custom technique is author-generated or created with the help of AI in some way is not entirely easy.
Ultimately, AI serves as a way to make malware developers’ jobs easier, allowing them to more easily put together code or scripts for a particular purpose. However, I’d say one of the most interesting – and potentially impactful – use of AI related to malware is when it’s used in a case like PROMPTSTEAL to alter its behavior mid-execution. I am certainly looking forward to seeing how AI changes how threat actors execute attacks, and understanding how we can more effectively defend against them.
If working exploit code can follow a disclosure within minutes, what happens to the patch window? Should defenders stop measuring response in days?
With the increased availability of AI, finding security flaws and vulnerabilities has not only become more accessible to and easier for people to do, but they can do it much more quickly and at scale. The PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities are a great example here, and had they been widely exploited by a threat actor instead of disclosed by security researchers, the damage could have been exceptional – especially before a patch was available.
Patching has been one of the most important tools for security teams to address vulnerabilities, especially those for which there are available exploits. It also brings with it some challenges that can often stretch the time teams take to implement them, notably versioning dependencies, ensuring the patch won’t break anything else, and downtime associated with putting the patch in. Time pressure around patching when a vulnerability becomes public (especially if it has publicly released POC exploits) has always been around, but now we’re facing more vulnerability disclosures on top of a very likely quicker and easier path to exploitability which serve to further narrow the time defenders have to mitigate it.
It’s challenging to give an exact timeframe for a patch window that would suit every organization, but we do know that we need to respond to the accelerating timelines created by AI-enabled threat actors.
Code was rarely the attacker’s bottleneck. Access, infrastructure and cashing out were. Where is AI changing criminal economics, and do you see it in dark web pricing for stolen accounts?
AI overall is lowering the barrier to entry for cybercriminals to conduct all kinds of fraud, including account-related fraud but a lot of the “benefit” we see today is in improving scalability, and increasing the efficiency of attacks. This materializes in a few different ways:
- Generation of “content”. This includes creating phishing pages/messages used to steal victims’ financial and personal information, conversing with victims of romance scams or pig butchering scams to reel them in, staging AI-written blog posts intended to hook a reader long enough to allow ads to load and reload, and audio tracks to enable streaming fraud.
- Going through large amounts of data to find data of interest. Data exfiltrated from stealers (which have been around long before AI, and remain popular methods of obtaining victim data), stolen from a company or scraped from a site contains swaths of information that AI can help structure or pick through to identify the most useful pieces. These might be usable session cookies and tokens from stolen browser data for session hijacking, valid credentials or files containing password data, any of which might be usable to escalate an attack, move laterally, or conduct a new one.
- Verifying data. One interesting case that we observed involved the use of an AI agent to conduct carding-like behavior. Traditionally, threat actors test credit card numbers to verify efficacy prior to selling them to other threat actors to conduct fraud. Verified cards can be sold for more than unverified ones.
In terms of pricing for accounts, I haven’t seen drastic changes that I can directly attribute to AI (pricing is largely based on supply and demand-related factors), but as noted, the economics of how these accounts are obtained and verified certainly represents an area in which AI provides a benefit to threat actors.
What should model providers share with threat intel teams that they don’t share now? Should abuse indicators from AI platforms flow the way IOCs do?
Honestly, I’d question whether “AI abuse indicator” is the right unit here. Similar to what I said earlier about reverse engineering, knowing a threat actor used AI is interesting context, but it isn’t usually the thing that helps me defend against them. What matters is what the activity does on the target.
That said, there’s real value in what already exists:
- Google and others have published research on threat actor usage of AI tools, which gives defenders a view into how these tools are being applied
- MITRE’s AI Incident Sharing Initiative, which sits within ATLAS, has stood up a STIX-based channel with a group of contributing organizations, and ATLAS has been adding generative AI techniques and case studies
To me, that’s a more useful direction than a separate indicator feed. An IOC is actionable because it’s specific and reasonably durable, a hash or domain. “A model was involved” is neither, and anything more granular, like a prompt pattern, tends to stop working the moment a model updates.
So if I had an ask, it would be about continuing to document the techniques, so they land in the frameworks teams already work from. That’s the format that reaches a detection engineer.
I’d also say this is a two-way conversation. Those of us seeing AI-enabled activity downstream have as much to contribute to that picture as platforms do.
How does your own team use AI in threat research, and where do you refuse to let a model make the call?
To date, my team has used AI as a way to augment our workflows. A great example is using AI to help summarize or ask questions from the data we collect from a wide variety of sources. In addition to data processing activities like extracting IOCs from reports that we may want to pivot on, we want to understand what tools are out there targeting our customers or products, whether they have changed since we last looked at them, and how these and other relevant topics are discussed in the underground forums we monitor.
AI can help us ask these kinds of questions and give initial answers to start from, but what it produces can’t be shared as-is without a human confirming the conclusions are correct and reviewing the findings from the lens of any additional insight we might have that the AI does not.
Another example is using AI as an aid for creating detection rules that we can use to hunt for additional malware related to samples of interest, or to help with clustering for samples or of disparate entities/groups based on commonalities in attributes. Again, AI serves as a way we can move more quickly towards developing our own analytical conclusions, but doesn’t replace that analytical layer provided by a human.

Lindsay Kaye of HUMAN Security explains how AI-generated malware exhibits distinct characteristics like structured comments and professional logging, while significantly accelerating the speed and scale of cyberattacks.

### Key Points
- AI-generated scripts often feature uniform, well-structured comments and professional logging messages that are atypical for traditional malware authors.
- Threat actors are using AI to rapidly scale advertising fraud, increasing the volume of malicious mobile apps and websites from dozens to hundreds.
- AI tools assist criminals in processing large datasets to identify valuable information, such as session cookies and credentials, for further exploitation.
- Automated agents are now being used to verify stolen credit card data, increasing the market value of compromised financial information.
- Security teams face a shrinking patch window as AI enables attackers to develop and deploy exploits for newly disclosed vulnerabilities much faster than before.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into the cybercrime ecosystem is forcing security professionals to rethink traditional defense strategies and incident response timelines. As attackers leverage automation to increase the speed and scale of their operations, organizations must prioritize human-led analysis to validate findings and mitigate risks effectively.

results.title: Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation
results.author: Mike Wheatley
results.content:
Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation
Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.
The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.
AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.
According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.
Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.
“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.
Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.
Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.
Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.
In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.
Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.
Kleiner Perkins’ Aditya Naganath said Traversal is the first company he has seen that brings “real intelligence” into complex production environments, and he’s confident there’s going to be enormous demand for it. “As AI dramatically accelerates the pace at which software is written and shipped, the complexity of managing production will only grow,” he predicted. “Traversal gives engineering teams the intelligence they need to understand their systems, resolve incidents faster and operate with confidence at scales that simply weren’t possible before.”

results.title: Democrats take control of Congress and put Trump's economic agenda in their sights
results.author: Ben Werschkul
results.content:
Democrats won control of Congress. Their economic agenda is set to target healthcare, tariffs, and Trump's allies.
Democrats retook power in Washington on Tuesday, flipping key House and Senate seats to command majorities in both chambers of Congress.
The power shift creates a new platform for Democrats to launch investigations of President Trump's economic allies — Elon Musk, to name one — and pass bills that may be unlikely to become law but will mark a sharp change in the political climate for business leaders and economic issues after two years of unified Republican control.
The change also appears set to elevate figures like Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others to prominent positions with oversight over economic policy.
Read more: What a Democratic sweep means for stocks
Democrats are planning "a shock-and-awe legislative sprint," the New York Times reported, on issues like healthcare subsidies and Trump's tariffs, which could prompt a wave of bills to pass the House but stall against the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. Even in the minority, Senate rules mean Republicans retain the power to stop legislation.
Democrats are also likely to seek areas of bipartisan agreement on pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers, all sectors that both Republicans and Democrats have spotlighted on the campaign trail.
Divided government, of course, may also set the stage for political clashes that could destabilize markets and the broader economy.
"While conventional wisdom suggests equities tend to rally following midterm elections, particularly when the outcome produces divided government, we caution that the post-election environment may look considerably different this cycle," Raymond James Washington Policy Analyst Ed Mills warned in a pre-election note.
He added that much of the recent volatility has been driven by unexpected moves from the White House. "We believe Trump will increasingly test the limits of executive authority during the remainder of his term," Mills wrote.
'Lawyer up': An expected focus on Elon Musk and Trump's economic team
The House is set to be led by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who has been notably tight-lipped about his plans.
He met with Democratic volunteers as Election Day wound down and told reporters, "We're relentlessly focused on driving down the high cost of living and fighting for an affordable America."
Jeffries avoided the question of whether he would reach out to Trump, while the president told the New York Times he will accept the election results.
Going by early signals, Democrats intend to aim their new powers at an array of high-profile targets, with Musk chief among them, as part of a far-reaching effort to impose new checks on the Trump administration.

### Key Points
- Democrats flipped key congressional seats to gain majorities in both the House and Senate, ending two years of unified Republican control.
- Incoming House leadership, including Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, plans to prioritize legislation addressing healthcare subsidies, tariff policies, and the cost of living.
- Congressional Democrats intend to use their new oversight powers to investigate President Trump’s economic team and high-profile allies, specifically naming Elon Musk.
- Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other Democrats are expected to take prominent roles in shaping economic policy and regulatory oversight.
- Despite the legislative shift, Republicans retain the ability to block major bills in the Senate due to the 60-vote threshold requirement.
- Potential bipartisan cooperation may emerge on issues involving pharmaceutical pricing, the housing market, and the development of AI data centers.

### Why it Matters
This shift to a divided government creates a new platform for political friction that could increase market volatility and test the limits of executive authority. While legislative progress may stall, the increased focus on oversight and investigations will likely force business leaders to navigate a more complex and adversarial regulatory environment.

TL;DR: Chainalysis disclosed a security incident on October 30 affecting a subset of customer-related information, including names, email addresses and certain user or role labels, according to the company. “No evidence of compromise” is not proof that a particular system was mathematically impossible to access.
The apparent boundary between identity information and investigative data is the central fact in this disclosure. Readers should not dismiss exposed contact details as harmless, but neither should they infer a breach of every product the company operates. Precision is particularly important when the firm itself works in cybercrime investigations.
What the primary source establishes
Chainalysis disclosed a security incident on October 30 affecting a subset of customer-related information, including names, email addresses and certain user or role labels, according to the company. It said there was no evidence that its investigative graph data, credentials or user sessions were compromised. This was a separate incident and should not be merged with Chainalysis’ analysis of the Binance theft. The dated original disclosure is the starting point for the figures and product scope discussed here.
Businesses that help investigate blockchain crime may also hold conventional personal and organisational information about their customers. Even when a breach does not expose transaction intelligence, names and roles can be useful to attackers crafting phishing or social-engineering messages. That risk depends on the exact data exposed and how those records can be combined with information already public.
Why this matters beyond the headline
The disclosure underscores the value of keeping customer identity systems, investigation data and access credentials in well-defined security boundaries. A malicious actor with one type of information should not automatically gain another. The company’s description can be used to understand the stated scope, but good incident response also includes validating those claims over time.
A crypto incident produces several separate timelines: containment, investigation, recovery and a return to reliable service. Those phases can overlap without finishing together. A traced wallet is not automatically frozen; a frozen balance is not automatically returned; and a reopened withdrawal route is not a completed security audit. Keeping those differences visible helps readers judge progress more accurately.
This development also connects to two subjects our newsroom has been following: Binance’s earlier staged withdrawal restart and Bitcoin payment infrastructure and node software context. Those background reports help separate established facts from a new, still-developing announcement.
What the announcement does not prove
“No evidence of compromise” is not proof that a particular system was mathematically impossible to access. It is a statement about what investigators had found as of the company’s update. Affected customers should rely on verified notices and avoid clicking unsolicited reset links. Equally, the existence of a data event does not prove that all users’ credentials were stolen.
Operational controls matter most when a business is under stress. Security announcements should identify the system affected, the customers who can act, the evidence supporting any recovery number and what remains uncertain. Clear scope protects users from false reassurance and from unnecessary panic. It also provides a sensible basis for follow-up accountability.
What to watch next
Next, look for the company’s follow-up findings, notice procedures and any confirmed misuse of exposed information. For organisations using investigative vendors, the broader lesson is that sensitive workflows should limit data sharing and use strong independent authentication. Vendor risk exists even when the core analytical product is technically sound.
This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the critical need for companies to maintain strict security boundaries between customer identity systems and sensitive investigative data. While the breach did not expose core blockchain intelligence, the leaked contact information increases the risk of targeted phishing and social engineering attacks against industry professionals.

results.title: Unraveling the Pentagon’s quantum problem
results.author: Lauren C. Williams
results.content:
Unraveling the Pentagon’s quantum problem
Defense agencies have just five years to comply with Executive Order 14412. The work starts with spreading awareness.
HONOLULU—Preparing for a quantum computer attack means two things: knowing exactly which systems will need to be upgraded and making sure everyone understands how serious the risk is to sensitive data protected by standard encryption.
“Our adversaries are using quantum. How advanced are their capabilities? We don't totally know. But the reality is that that presents some threats, and the challenge with, you know, post-quantum cryptography is this idea of ‘harvest now, decrypt later,’” said Matt McFadden, vice president of cyber for GDIT, during a panel discussion at the TechNet Info-Pacific conference here. “The reality is, with ‘harvest now, decrypt later,’ our adversaries can be harvesting data for a really, really long time,” and eventually a quantum computer will be able to break the standard encryption used today.
Post-quantum cryptography, or the mathematical algorithms needed to secure networks and systems from attacks using quantum computers, is a challenge each military service must tackle. But the White House put a timeline on it for federal agencies—by Dec. 31, 2030—for high value assets and high-impact systems “to use PQC for key establishment” in an executive order issued June 22. The deadline “to use PQC for digital signatures” is 2031.
“It’s just this one more threat vector that we have to be concerned about as we develop our resilient architecture,” said Col. Tassika Davis, Pacific Air Forces Command’s director of cyber operations and warfighter communications. “Now, we need to make sure that our architectures are cryptographically agile, so that we can shift and move and continue, and not degrade mission capability, while we are also providing the most current defense capabilities.”
To do that takes mapping the whole IT ecosystem as it is, “looking at it from the entire threat picture, and then planning against that,” she said.
It sounds simple but just knowing what exactly needs to be protected is a key, yet challenging first step, GDIT’s McFadden said during the panel.
“It's hard to migrate when you don't know what you have. So, really, the first step in this process is really having a comprehensive inventory,” he said, including certifications for apps, devices, and networks. “One of the things you realize pretty fast is like you're very reliant on third-party providers…you’ve got to really work together with the system owners, the third-party suppliers, your supply chains, and basically build that governance team to help drive” compliance and crypto agility, or the ability to combat quantum cyber threats.
Securing systems for a post-quantum threat becomes more complicated when the platforms that need to be upgraded don’t stay in one place for long.
“Ships are being extended more than they have been. There are crises that are popping up everywhere. And we used to be in a period of [maintenance] availabilities, which means we had about nine months to a year to do modernization. Now you’ve got 45 days,” said Capt. Victor Taylor, Pacific Fleet’s director of communications and information systems, during the panel. “So, how do I break up these big pieces of modernization into modular…shorter windows? How do I execute the configuration management? How do I have the teams to do it at scale at multiple locations? And then how do I schedule it with all the dynamic changes that are occurring? And so, if we think we're going to do that with our old processes, that's not the case.”
And part of the Pentagon and military services upgrading their high-value systems to withstand a quantum attack will be making sure individuals are aware of the quantum threat.
“The first thing is to acknowledge that it's a real problem. Like Q-Day isn't a thing that's going to be beyond our retirement. Q-Day is going to be a thing that happens…definitely within the next five years,” Peter O’Donoghue, Quantum Sky’s chief technology officer, told Defense One after the panel. “So, then you need to plan for it. You need to actually fund it.”
